France’s file stands at midday exactly where the midnight file left it, and the desk records the standing. The police firearms law—adopted by the Senate on Friday by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting—creates a rebuttable presumption that national police officers and gendarmes used their firearms lawfully, amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code, and leaves every use required to be absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate, in the text account filed below. It has not been promulgated and has not entered into force; the Socialist, Ecologist and Republican group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation; no filing of the referral stands in the midday file, and promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized, in the same account. On the Landes coast the second ship of the week’s file is also standing still: the Miro G lies where she grounded, her main generators unavailable, complicating efforts to pump ballast water, and shallow water could keep a rescue tug nearly 3,000 feet away, in the beach account filed below, which records the prefecture’s caution that a refloating attempt might take days or longer and that its success cannot yet be guaranteed; the navy’s assessment team, the two tugs mobilized under the response and the Biscay Plan, and the plan to lighten the ship of her diesel and lubricants stand in the tracking account filed below. No pollution has been detected around her in either account. Settled: the law’s text and the bulker’s position. Open: the referral, and the refloating.

The air’s midday file is a planning list, not a stop, and the desk prints it as one. The aviation administration’s operations plan, issued at 1004 UTC, reported no active ground stops at the eight airports its Saturday risk list names—Miami, Fort Lauderdale, Orlando, Tampa, Austin, San Antonio, Seattle and San Diego—and its national summary updated at 1159 UTC showed none either, in the planning account filed below; Austin carries the strongest signal, a ground stop or delay programme described as expected after 6 a.m. Central, the Florida airports face possible stops after noon Eastern, and a separate LaGuardia delay programme stands scheduled for the afternoon on construction, in the same account. A tracker built on the same national feed, stamped at 9:01 a.m. Eastern, shows one active ground stop, two delay programmes, two closures and seven airports affected across the country, with disruption severity down 32 percent against the prior week, in the tracker account filed below. Ahead of the file stands the holiday week: Los Angeles expects nearly 2.6 million passengers between November 19 and 30, in the planning account, and the Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers on the November 13 ground stop on November 23. The root cause itself stands unannounced at midday, nine days after the stop. Settled: the plan, and the absence of a stop at the eight named airports at the plan’s hour. Open: the afternoon’s weather and traffic, and the root cause.

 SubjectiveHouse of Saud — 2 Tankers Hit by Projectiles Near Hormuz, Iran Claims MinesThe United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre issued two separate attack warnings within 50 minutes on November 21: Warning 215-26, at about 0500 UTC, a tanker struck on its stern by an unknown projectile 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, and Warning 216-26, 50 minutes later, a second outbound tanker struck in its engine room 17 nautical miles east of Khasab.  SubjectiveBars Across — France Approves Rebuttable Presumption for Police Firearms UseFrance has approved a bill creating a rebuttable presumption that national police officers and gendarmes used their firearms lawfully. The Senate adopted it on November 20 by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting; the National Assembly approved the text in July. It amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code and permits firearms use in five situations, each still required to be absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate; the presumption covers national police and gendarmes, not municipal police. An opinion of November 5 from the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s democracy office recommended reconsidering the measure. The Socialist, Ecologist and Republican group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation; no court has ruled on its constitutionality, and promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized.

 SubjectiveSurfer — 554-Foot Cargo Ship Stranded on French Beach (Video)The Miro G, a Malta-flagged bulk carrier of 554 feet, ran aground on France’s Atlantic coast early Friday, November 20, near Lit-et-Mixe, planted in the sand while Atlantic swell pounds its hull. Nineteen of its 22 crew were airlifted off; the captain and two crew members stayed aboard. The ship is not moving at present, but as the tide changes it could become unstable, and that is when the risk of capsizing arises, a maritime prefecture spokesman told France 3. The ship carries more than 100 tons of diesel fuel, and an initial aerial survey found no pollution. By Saturday, authorities warned a refloating attempt might take days or longer: the ship’s main generators were unavailable, complicating efforts to pump ballast water, and shallow water could keep a rescue tug nearly 3,000 feet away; the prefecture cautioned that the operation’s success cannot yet be guaranteed.

 SubjectiveVesselTracker — Maritime Insights: the Miro G groundingBallasting from Bayonne to Rouen with 22 crew on board, the Miro G ran aground on the Landes coast near Lit-et-Mixe in the early morning of November 20, after reporting manoeuvring difficulties on the evening of November 19 and dragging both anchors in gusts of 48 knots from an emergency anchorage 1.8 nautical miles offshore, coming to rest at 44 degrees 02 minutes north, 001 degrees 21 minutes west. Nineteen non-essential crew were evacuated by helicopter and taken to shelter at Saint-Julien-en-Born; three remained aboard. The Maritime Prefect of the Atlantic activated the third level of the maritime response plan, the Franco-Spanish Biscay Plan was activated and the Spanish tug Sar Gavia sailed from Bilbao, though heavy swells prevented it intervening; the Brest tug Abeille Bretagne also sailed in anticipation of a refloating operation. A navy assessment team was deployed by helicopter to study refloating options, a surveillance aircraft identified no pollution, and it was expected the ship would have to be lightened, its diesel and lubricants removed, to be moved again.

 SubjectiveTravel and Tour World — Miami and Seven Other US Cities Face Saturday FAA Ground Stop Risks Ahead of ThanksgivingThe Federal Aviation Administration has identified potential disruptions affecting Miami, Fort Lauderdale, Orlando, Tampa, Austin, San Antonio, Seattle and San Diego on Saturday, November 21. Its operations plan issued at 1004 UTC reported no active ground stops at these airports, and its national status summary updated at 1159 UTC also showed no ground stops affecting the eight. Austin faces the strongest planning signal, a ground stop or delay programme described as expected after 6 a.m. Central; the Florida airports face possible ground stops after 12 p.m. Eastern; Seattle and San Diego face possible programmes after 9 a.m. Pacific. The summary also listed a separate LaGuardia ground delay programme scheduled between 1400 and 1759 UTC, associated with runway and taxiway construction. The account notes that Los Angeles expects nearly 2.6 million passengers between November 19 and 30.

 SubjectiveReroute — Thanksgiving 2026 Flight Cancellation Tracker, Live FAA DataAs of Saturday, November 21, the tracker, built on the Federal Aviation Administration’s national status feed and stamped at 9:01 a.m. Eastern, shows one active ground stop, two ground delay programmes, two airport closures and seven airports affected across the United States, heading into the November 26 to 30 peak. In the week ending Saturday, the tracker recorded disruptions on seven of seven days, with the John Wayne, San Francisco and San Diego airports the hardest hit, and disruption severity down 32 percent against the prior week. The account states that the feed reports by airport, not by airline, and that its rankings aggregate the rolling seven-day history of its checks.

### Venice Closes in Minor Keys, Abu Dhabi Opens Under Frieze, and Ayutthaya Lights Its First Krathongs

Filed as: Saturday Culture Feature — Weekend Features · 2026-11-21T04:10:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-21-saturday-culture.html

Weekend Features — Saturday Culture

 Objective

 Venice Closes in Minor Keys, Abu Dhabi Opens Under Frieze, and Ayutthaya Lights Its First Krathongs

 Three closings stand on one Sunday and four openings stand within four days of them: Venice ends six months in minor keys, Abu Dhabi ends its first four days under a new name, and Tallinn ends its thirtieth festival, while Tokyo opens a museum by sound, Dublin opens a sea borrowed from Sharjah, Sharjah opens an architecture triennial and closes a calligraphy biennial down to its smallest dot, and Thailand floats the first krathongs of its full-moon week at Ayutthaya. The desk files the week in that order.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Saturday, November 21, 2026. The third Saturday Culture Feature of this paper, filed ahead of the day's watches under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. International by house rule: no country's framework is applied to another country's culture. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief

Three of the year’s longest cultural runs end on the same Sunday, and the week’s openings are dated to the day on either side of them: the 61st Venice Biennale, open since May 9, closes on November 22; the first Frieze Abu Dhabi, open since November 19, closes on November 22; and Tallinn’s 30th Black Nights festival, open since November 6, closes on November 22. Against those three endings the file carries four beginnings inside four days: Tokyo’s Museum of Narratives opened its first exhibition, Feel the Sound, on Friday, November 20; Dublin’s Irish Museum of Modern Art opened A Sea for Borrowed Time, drawn from the Sharjah Art Foundation collection, on Thursday, November 19; Sharjah’s third Architecture Triennial, open since November 14, closed its six-day opening programme on November 19 and runs to April 14, 2027; and in Thailand three Loi Krathong festivals open today, November 21, at Ayutthaya, Tak and Samut Songkhram, inside a national calendar that ends at the full moon on November 24.

Venice: Six Months End on Sunday, at Five Euros

The 61st International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, titled In Minor Keys by Koyo Kouoh, runs from May 9 to Sunday, November 22, at the Giardini and the Arsenale, in locations across Venice and at Forte Marghera, and this Saturday stands in its final weekend. The Biennale’s own page, filed below, counts 110 invited participants and 100 National Participations, 29 in the historic Pavilions at the Giardini, 25 at the Arsenale and 46 in the city centre, with seven countries participating for the first time and El Salvador participating for the first time with its own pavilion; 31 Collateral Events stand across the city. The exhibition is the one Koyo Kouoh conceived: the Biennale records that, with the full support of her family, it carried out her exhibition following the project just as she conceived and defined it. The final ten days, from November 13 to November 22, carry a public programme of performances, lectures, discussions and roundtables at the Arsenale, with an Assembly of ten artist-led organisations and collectives. The closing is priced for the city that hosts it: admission today is &euro;5 for residents of the Comune di Venezia, the metropolitan area and the Veneto region, and on Sunday it is &euro;5 for all visitors, in the Biennale’s own listing filed below. Two Visitors’ Lions stand established for this edition in the same listing; the desk files the establishment and does not file a result, because none stands in the record at the stamp.

Inside the Giardini, one installation states the edition’s method in built form. Chimera brings together contributions from approximately 150 artists associated with Denniston Hill, the artist-founded cultural laboratory founded in 2004, presented as part of In Minor Keys, in the university account filed below. Its structure is the Exquisite Corpse: alumni artists made works for parts of a collective body, the head for dreams and invention, the torso for voice and transformation, the legs for movement, migration and journeys into the future, without seeing the whole. The setting, designed by Koray Duman, centres on an arena-like gathering space with the works on totem-like armatures, in a passage between the bookstore and the restrooms that the account’s subjects describe as a social condenser. The team also ran an indigo-dye workshop with artists who work with dyers in rural northeast Thailand, and the account records that the magazine frieze named the contribution among the exhibition’s most compelling realisations of Kouoh’s vision. A six-month exhibition ends, in this corner of it, as a body assembled by 150 people who never saw it whole.

Abu Dhabi: A First Frieze, Sold by the Hour

The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi runs at Manarat Al Saadiyat from November 19 to Sunday, November 22, and its first public days have produced a record of sales made inside hours. The fair is organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi, in partnership with Frieze, and it replaces Abu Dhabi Art, founded in 2009; it was opened by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, in the Media Office account filed below, which presents the edition as building on Abu Dhabi Art’s 17 years and as the emirate’s entry into Frieze’s network of fairs in London, New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Seoul. The ground reports count 89 exhibitors against 142 at Abu Dhabi Art last year, in the Artnet report and in the Ocula report, both filed below; the disagreement in the fair’s counts is filed whole in the Cocked Hat. Around 40 percent of exhibitors are from West Asia, North Africa and South Asia, and the fair’s director, Dyala Nusseibeh, who previously directed Abu Dhabi Art, calls the partnership a step change in how art from the region is understood, in the Artnet account.

The Masters section sold the fair’s oldest objects first. David Aaron, one of nine Masters galleries showing under the theme of the Indian Ocean as a historic avenue for trade, sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele naming a woman from Qataban, in modern-day Yemen, for seven figures within the first few hours, the work’s first return to the Arabian Peninsula in 70 years, in the Artnet account; the Ocula account describes the same object as a yellow-calcite alabaster stele from ancient Yemen, its sale pre-agreed, and adds a second seven-figure-class sale, Daniel Crouch Rare Books’ first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated 1832, at an asking price understood to exceed $1 million. Around those sales the reports price the contemporary floor: Timothy Taylor sold out its presentation of Hilary Pecis at $65,000 to $205,000; a Sheila Hicks textile went at $350,000; Pace prices Emily Kam Kngwarray up to $750,000; and Efie Gallery anchors its booth with El Anatsui hangings at $525,000 to $1.8 million. The fair’s own commission stands outside the booths: Dala Nasser’s Qubbat Duris, the Artist Award work, encases a recreation of an architectural ruin in southern Lebanon in earthen-hued textile paintings. Both ground reports also file the conditions: flight paths disrupted and some plans cancelled in the Ocula account, attendance better than expected in the same account, and the fair’s chief executive on the record in the Artnet account that the fair is in it for the long haul. The edition closes on Sunday, two days shorter than its predecessor ran.

Tallinn: 489 Titles End on Sunday

The 30th Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, POFF, runs in Tallinn and Tartu from November 6 to Sunday, November 22, and its arithmetic is exact: 230 feature films and 259 shorts sum to the 489 titles its programme release announces, from 87 countries, with 107 world premieres and 47 international premieres across the festival and its Just Film and POFF Shorts strands, in the programme release filed below. The anniversary edition places the region at its centre: Focus: Baltics brings Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into sharper view, presenting recent Baltic films and the teams behind them, in the Baltic Review account filed below. The festival began in 1997 and has held the International Federation of Film Producers Associations’ accreditation since 2014, in the same account, which records its standing as one of Northern Europe’s largest festivals and the region’s only accredited competitive feature festival. Its industry arm has already closed: Industry@Tallinn and Baltic Event, in its 25th edition, ran from November 9 to 20 and expected nearly 2,000 guests from more than 50 countries, in the programme release. The anniversary stands in the city as well as in the cinemas: the Estonian animator Priit P&auml;rn made its design, and a commemorative stamp and a tram carrying the festival’s artwork mark the year, in the Baltic Review account. What remains at the stamp is two days of screenings in two cities, and then the festival’s thirtieth year is a record.

Tokyo: A Museum Opens by Sound

MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives in Minato, Tokyo, opened Feel the Sound on Friday, November 20, as its opening commemorative programme, and the exhibition runs to March 22, 2027. The museum stands inside Takanawa Gateway City at 3-16-1 Mita and is operated by the East Japan Railway Foundation for Cultural Innovations, in the MANA account filed below. The exhibition is co-produced with the Barbican Centre in London, where it ran from May 22 to August 31, 2025; this presentation is its first in Japan, and the Tokyo edition carries new adaptations of existing works and three new works made for the occasion, in the MANA account and in the NiEW account filed below. Its premise is stated in its poster’s tagline, rendered in the MANA account as: that sound reaches the body before the ear. The installations combine sound, vibration and light, and the featured list opens with Sensing Streams, invisible, inaudible: focused edition, 2025, by Ryuichi Sakamoto and Daito Manabe, which turns electromagnetic waves beyond human perception into sound and light; Max Cooper, Miyu Hosoi, Ei Wada and Yuri Suzuki stand among the featured artists. The museum keeps late hours for the opening weekend’s second day: 10:00 to 19:00 ordinarily, and until 21:00 on Fridays and Saturdays, with regular tickets at 2,500 yen, 1,100 yen for visitors aged 25 and under, and 550 yen for elementary to high-school students, in the MANA account. Where Venice closes a six-month exhibition this weekend, Tokyo opens a four-month one, on the same Saturday, at the opposite end of the same trade in attention.

Sharjah: A Triennial in Its First Week, a Biennial in Its Last Room

Sharjah holds two positions in the week at once: a beginning and an ending, in two different art forms. The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, curated by Vyjayanthi Rao with associate curator Tau Tavengwa, opened on November 14 and runs to April 14, 2027, across the Emirate; its opening programme ran from November 14 to 19, bringing 35 international participants together in installations, participatory projects, performances, film screenings, lectures and panel discussions, and closed with a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19, in the ArchDaily listing filed below. The Triennial’s proposition, as the listing states it, is that architecture fosters collective life through social relationships, shared knowledge and civic engagement, and the exhibition now stands open for five months on that proposition. The ending is calligraphic. The 12th Sharjah Calligraphy Biennial, organised under the theme Balance, closed its main run on November 15; its final stop, the exhibition In Due Measure: From Dot to Meaning at the House of Wisdom, opened on November 11 and runs to January 24, 2027, in the UAE News account filed below. The exhibition builds its subject from its smallest unit: five sections carry the visitor from the dot that measures every letter, through the letter, the word and the sentence, to contemporary practices beyond measure, with the pioneers of the proportional system, Ibn Muqla, Ibn al-Bawwab and Yaqut al-Musta’simi, introduced beside the contemporary hands, and tables where visitors draw the dots and practise the letters themselves. One emirate therefore files both ends of the season in the same week: an architecture exhibition with five months to run, and a calligraphy exhibition reduced, deliberately, to the dot it began from.

Dublin: A Sea Borrowed From Sharjah

The Irish Museum of Modern Art opened A Sea for Borrowed Time in its House Galleries on Thursday, November 19, and the exhibition runs to July 4, 2027, with free admission. It is a major exhibition of contemporary Palestinian art made in partnership with Sharjah Art Foundation and drawn from that foundation’s collection, curated by Hoor Al Qasimi, in the museum’s announcement filed below. Eight artists stand in the show, Tarek Al-Ghoussein, Basma Al Sharif, Simone Fattal, Shadi Habib Allah, Rula Halawani, Hazem Harb, Khalil Rabah and Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara, spanning three generations and working in photography, sculpture, installation, film and painting; the exhibition moves between testimony, memory, lived experience and imagination rather than following a chronology. Its objects carry their histories in plain terms in the announcement: Fattal’s lava stone inscribed with locations in Palestine and Lebanon associated with massacres; Harb’s work centred on the suitcase he carried when he left Gaza in 2006; Halawani’s photographs of everyday movement through military checkpoints, commissioned by the Sharjah Art Foundation in 2017. At the centre of the Zarara focus stands a relief connected to Ireland, discovered in the artist’s studio shortly before his death in 2020 and shown publicly for the first time in this exhibition. A collection assembled in Sharjah thus opens in Dublin in the same week Sharjah itself opens an architecture triennial and closes a calligraphy biennial: the week’s map has Sharjah at three of its points.

Thailand: Three Festivals Open Today

Thailand’s Loi Krathong calendar reaches its full moon on Tuesday, November 24, and three of its festivals open today, Saturday, November 21. The festival centres on floating decorated krathongs as an expression of gratitude and respect for water, observed on the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month, in the nationwide calendar filed below. The principal venue this year is Ayutthaya, the former royal capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, where the festival runs from November 21 to 24 at the Ancient Palace grounds near Wat Phra Si Sanphet, in the Tourism Authority’s announcement filed below. Ayutthaya revives Chong Priang, an ancient royal tradition of ceremonial lantern-lighting, and centres its nights on Saeng Nathi Si Sanphet, a 45-minute production of light, sound and theatre animating 417 years of the city’s history, performed nightly at 7:30 p.m. before 1,000 complimentary seats; admission is free from 4:30 to 10:00 p.m., a period-style market carries more than 70 local vendors, and today’s opening ceremony recreates an Ayutthaya-era lantern procession. At Tak, the Loi Krathong Sai festival opens today on the Ping River and runs to November 24, its signature a competition of 1,000 illuminated krathongs floating in continuous streams. At Samut Songkhram, the Mae Klong festival opens today on the Tourism Authority’s dates and will float more than 100,000 krathongs made from banana stalks on the Mae Klong River; the nationwide calendar’s dating of the same festival is filed in the Cocked Hat. Around the three openings the calendar is already running: Sukhothai’s candlelight festival has run at the Historical Park since November 15 and ends on the full-moon night; Bangkok’s Rattanakosin Waterways programme runs from November 17 to 29; Chiang Mai’s Yi Peng follows from November 23 to 25, with authorised sky lantern releases on November 24 and 25; and the Authority states its expectation for the period at approximately 6 billion baht of domestic tourism revenue, up 8 percent, on an estimated 1.83 million domestic trips, up 6 percent, in the announcement. The expectation is the Authority’s; the openings are today’s.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the size of the first Frieze Abu Dhabi: 84 galleries from 64 cities across 37 countries in the Experience Abu Dhabi listing; more than 85 galleries from 67 cities and more than 35 countries and regions in the fair’s own line-up release of October 22; and 89 exhibitors counted in each of the two opening reports from the ground, Artnet and Ocula. The desk prints each count as its source’s and merges none of them; the comparison both ground reports agree on, 142 galleries at Abu Dhabi Art last year, stands uncontradicted. Second, the fair’s opening day: the fair is dated November 19 to 22 in every source, the Media Office records the Crown Prince opening the fair, and the Artnet report records the fair as opened to the public at the stamp of its filing; the dated run and the public admission are both in the file, and the desk does not collapse them into one day. Third, Venice’s counts: 110 invited participants and 100 National Participations stand on the Biennale’s own page, and those are the figures the desk prints; a foundation release in the week’s wider coverage counts 111 invited participants, and the difference of one stands unresolved in the file. Fourth, Samut Songkhram: the Tourism Authority’s announcement of November 18 dates the Mae Klong festival from November 21 to 24, and the Authority’s nationwide calendar lists its banana-stem festival on November 24; the desk prints the announcement’s run for the festival’s opening today and the calendar’s date beside it, unreconciled. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: the Venice Biennale runs May 9 to November 22 in its 61st edition under the title In Minor Keys; Frieze Abu Dhabi runs November 19 to 22 at Manarat Al Saadiyat in its inaugural edition; Tallinn’s 30th festival runs November 6 to 22 with 230 features and 259 shorts; Feel the Sound opened in Tokyo on November 20 and runs to March 22, 2027; the Sharjah Architecture Triennial runs November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, and In Due Measure runs at the House of Wisdom to January 24, 2027; A Sea for Borrowed Time opened in Dublin on November 19 and runs to July 4, 2027; and Loi Krathong’s full moon is November 24, with its Ayutthaya, Tak and Samut Songkhram festivals opening on November 21. The log proceeds to Saturday’s watches.

 The Clippings Filed With This Feature

 Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective — a source with a position, printed because it is useful — and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. Sixteen items.

 SubjectiveSyracuse University Today — Chimera, a collective body of 150 artists, in the GiardiniVenice, November 16: as the 61st International Art Exhibition approaches its November 22 conclusion, the collaborative installation Chimera, by Lawrence Chua, associate professor in the School of Architecture, and his colleagues, is drawing international attention; the installation brings together contributions from approximately 150 artists associated with Denniston Hill, the artist-founded cultural laboratory Chua co-founded in 2004 with artists Julie Mehretu and Paul Pfeiffer, and is presented as part of this year's exhibition, In Minor Keys, in Venice's historic Giardini; it is inspired by the Surrealist parlour game the Exquisite Corpse, in which participants contribute fragments to a collective composition without seeing the whole, with the head representing dreams and invention, the torso voice and transformation, and the legs movement, migration and journeys into the future; the physical setting, designed by architect Koray Duman, founder of B-KD, centres on an arena-like gathering space, with individual artworks displayed on totem-like armatures; the Biennale assigned Denniston Hill an interstitial space between the bookstore and restrooms in the Giardini pavilion, along the passage connecting the national pavilions and cafe; the team also organised an indigo-dye workshop with artists Philip Huang and Chomwan Weeraworawit, who work with local dyers in rural northeast Thailand; and the account records that the magazine frieze, in its review of In Minor Keys, highlighted Denniston Hill's contribution as one of the exhibition's most compelling realisations of the vision of the late artistic director Koyo Kouoh.

 SubjectiveOcula — Frieze Abu Dhabi opens with optimismAbu Dhabi, November 20: Frieze made its Middle Eastern debut yesterday at Manarat Al Saadiyat, running through Sunday, amid a busy month for culture in the United Arab Emirates that also carries the art and design showcase NOMAD and the ongoing Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial; the account records that the war in Iran has escalated military tensions across the Gulf and disrupted some regional flight paths, that some plans were cancelled, and that first-day attendance was better than expected regionally and internationally; director Dyala Nusseibeh, who previously directed Abu Dhabi Art, now overseen by Frieze in partnership with the Department of Culture and Tourism, said it is very much business as usual and that Abu Dhabi is a very safe and secure place; in Frieze Masters, David Aaron announced the pre-agreed, seven-figure sale of a yellow-calcite alabaster stele from ancient Yemen, and Daniel Crouch Rare Books sold the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832, for an undisclosed asking price understood to be in excess of $1 million; Timothy Taylor sold out its solo presentation of Hilary Pecis, priced between $65,000 and $205,000; the Paris-based galerie frank elbaz sold a $350,000 textile work by Sheila Hicks to a private collection in the region; Thaddaeus Ropac placed three sculptures by Imran Qureshi, priced at $60,000 each, with collections in the Emirates; the fair's Artist Award commission, Dala Nasser's Qubbat Duris, 2026, encases a recreation of an architectural ruin in southern Lebanon in earthen-hued textile paintings; the account counts 89 exhibitors, records that the fair runs two days shorter than its predecessor, Abu Dhabi Art, and reports Sotheby's figure of a 70 percent increase in bidding from the Middle East over the past five years, Christie's first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi earlier this month at $8.9 million, and Sotheby's own Abu Dhabi auction to follow next month.

 SubjectiveBaltic Review — POFF30 puts Baltic cinema at the centre of Estonia's film seasonTallinn, November 17: the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, known by its Estonian acronym POFF, is giving Baltic cinema a particularly prominent place in Estonia's cultural calendar this November, running from November 6 to 22, 2026, in Tallinn and Tartu; this year's central regional initiative is Focus: Baltics, bringing Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into sharper view and presenting recent Baltic films, intended not only to showcase finished films but also to support the region's next generation of filmmakers; POFF began in 1997 and has grown into one of Northern Europe's largest film festivals, holding accreditation from the International Federation of Film Producers Associations since 2014; its industry event, Industry@Tallinn and Baltic Event, is holding its 25th edition during the same period; alongside the main competition the festival includes Just Film, its youth and children's programme, and POFF Shorts, dedicated to short and animated films; the festival has connected its visual identity with Estonian animation by inviting filmmaker and artist Priit Parn to create the anniversary design, and the organisers have highlighted the festival's history through a commemorative stamp and a Tallinn tram carrying POFF-related artwork; and the anniversary programme continues through November 22, with screenings in Tallinn and a parallel programme in Tartu.

 SubjectiveNiEW — Feel the Sound opens at MoN Takanawa, Tokyo, November 20Tokyo: Feel the Sound, an immersive exhibition exploring the experience of sound beyond hearing, opens at MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives in Tokyo, on November 20, 2026, and runs through March 22, 2027; co-produced with London's Barbican Centre, the exhibition comes to Japan for the first time following its London debut in 2025, and, combining sound, vibration and light, its installations offer visitors new ways to experience sound through their entire bodies; the Tokyo edition brings together works from the original Barbican exhibition, reimagined versions of existing installations and three new works created for the occasion; featured artists include Ryuichi Sakamoto, Daito Manabe, Max Cooper, Miyu Hosoi, Ei Wada and Yuri Suzuki; one highlight is Sensing Streams, invisible, inaudible: focused edition, 2025, a collaboration between Sakamoto and Manabe that turns electromagnetic waves beyond human perception into sound and light; the venue is MoN Takanawa, Box1500, on the fifth floor, at 3-16-1 Mita, Minato-ku, Tokyo, inside Takanawa Gateway City; and tickets are available through the museum's website and ArtSticker, with advance booking required.

 SubjectiveMANA — Feel the Sound opens at MoN Takanawa, with the Tokyo edition's particularsTokyo, November 19: tomorrow, November 20, 2026, MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives, presents the Japan premiere of Feel the Sound, an immersive sound exhibition co-produced with London's Barbican Centre, on view through March 22, 2027, in Box1500; the museum, at 3-16-1 Mita, Minato-ku, Tokyo, inside Takanawa Gateway City, is operated by the East Japan Railway Foundation for Cultural Innovations; the official press release of November 4, 2026, issued with the Barbican Centre, announces the Japan first presentation of Feel the Sound, the immersive exhibition that ran at the Barbican from May 22 to August 31, 2025, with MoN Takanawa as organiser and co-producer and the original concept and production the Barbican's; the Tokyo edition includes new adaptations of existing works and three new works added specially for this presentation; the poster's Japanese tagline is rendered in the account as: that sound reaches the body before the ear; opening hours are 10:00 to 19:00, and until 21:00 on Fridays and Saturdays, with last entry 30 minutes before closing; advance tickets, on sale from October 30 to November 19, were 2,300 yen general, 900 yen for ages 25 and under, and 350 yen for elementary to high-school students, and regular prices from November 20 are 2,500 yen, 1,100 yen and 550 yen; and the official featured list opens with Sensing Streams, invisible, inaudible: focused edition, 2025, by Ryuichi Sakamoto and Daito Manabe.

 SubjectiveArchDaily — Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026, November 14 to April 14Sharjah, November 10: the third edition of the Sharjah Architecture Triennial, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, curated by Vyjayanthi Rao with associate curator Tau Tavengwa, takes place across the Emirate of Sharjah from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027; the opening programme, November 14 to 19, brings together 35 international participants to explore how architecture can foster collective life through social relationships, shared knowledge and civic engagement; the six-day programme features installations, participatory projects, performances, film screenings, lectures and panel discussions, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19, 2026; and the Triennial's listed venue address is 7 Sheikh Saqr Bin Khalid Al Qasimi Street, Al Manakh, Sharjah.

 SubjectiveUAE News 24/7 — In Due Measure, the Calligraphy Biennial's closing exhibition, at the House of WisdomSharjah, November 11: the House of Wisdom in Sharjah has opened In Due Measure: From Dot to Meaning, an exhibition exploring the geometric and aesthetic foundations of Arabic calligraphy and the precise principles of measurement and proportion that shape Arabic letters, from the dot, the alif and the circle to the formation of words and sentences; running until January 24, 2027, the exhibition marks the final stop of the 12th Sharjah Calligraphy Biennial, organised by the Sharjah Department of Culture under the theme Balance; it presents calligraphic artworks, reproductions of historic Qur'an manuscripts and traditional writing tools across five sections, The Dot: Unit of Measurement, The Letter: Geometry of Beauty, The Word: Rhythm and Composition, The Sentence: From Composition to Meaning, and Beyond Measure: Contemporary Practices; it introduces the pioneers of Arabic calligraphy, Ibn Muqla, associated with establishing the foundations of proportional calligraphy, and Ibn al-Bawwab and Yaqut al-Musta'simi; its works are by Sheikha Khawla Bint Ahmed Bin Khalifa Al Suwaidi, calligraphers Khalid Al Jallaf, Khalifa Al Shimi and Humaid Al Saadi, and Ali Al Hammadi, alongside a sculpture by Nasser Al Salem from the Barjeel Art Foundation collection; and at its Dot and Pen Table and Letter-Writing Table, visitors can draw dots of different sizes to explore letter proportions and follow video demonstrations into guided writing exercises.

 SubjectiveIMMA — A Sea for Borrowed Time opens in Dublin, November 19 to July 4Dublin, November 9: the Irish Museum of Modern Art presents A Sea for Borrowed Time, a major exhibition of contemporary Palestinian art in partnership with Sharjah Art Foundation, in the House Galleries from November 19, 2026, to July 4, 2027, with free admission; bringing together works by Tarek Al-Ghoussein, Basma Al Sharif, Simone Fattal, Shadi Habib Allah, Rula Halawani, Hazem Harb, Khalil Rabah and Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara, drawn from the Sharjah Art Foundation collection, the exhibition examines how contemporary artists have responded to histories of political resistance, displacement, occupation, memory and solidarity through photography, sculpture, installation, film and painting; it moves between testimony, memory, lived experience and imagination rather than following a chronological approach, spanning three generations; Simone Fattal's In Our Lands of Drought the Rain Forever is Made of Bullets, 2006, inscribes lava stone with locations in Palestine and Lebanon associated with massacres; Hazem Harb's Sustainable Waiting, 2012, centres on the suitcase he carried when he left Gaza in 2006; Rula Halawani's photographic series The Bride is Beautiful but she is married to another man, 2017, commissioned by the Sharjah Art Foundation, documents everyday movement through military checkpoints; the exhibition includes a major focus on Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara, 1933 to 2020, whose relief connected to Ireland was discovered in the artist's studio shortly before his death and is shown publicly for the first time; and the exhibition is organised by IMMA and Sharjah Art Foundation and curated by Hoor Al Qasimi.

 SubjectiveTAT Newsroom — Loi Krathong 2026, led by Ayutthaya, November 21 to 24Bangkok, November 18: the Tourism Authority of Thailand has announced its Loi Krathong 2026 celebrations, led by the Ayutthaya Loi Krathong Festival 2026 from November 21 to 24, with support for five other provincial celebrations in Chiang Mai, Sukhothai, Tak, Samut Songkhram and Roi Et, complementing celebrations across Thailand during the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month; Ayutthaya, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and former royal capital, is the principal venue, and the festival is staged at the Ancient Palace grounds near Wat Phra Si Sanphet in Ayutthaya Historical Park under the theme Chong Priang Loi Khom Chom Wang Si Ayutthaya; it centres on Saeng Nathi Si Sanphet, a 45-minute light, sound and theatrical production animating 417 years of Ayutthaya's history, performed nightly at 7:30 p.m. with 1,000 complimentary seats, 500 reservable online and 500 available at the venue from 5:00 p.m.; admission is free from 4:30 to 10:00 p.m. daily; the festival revives Chong Priang, an ancient royal tradition of ceremonial lantern-lighting, alongside the floating of krathongs, with a period-style market of more than 70 local vendors, and its opening ceremony on November 21 features a recreation of an Ayutthaya-era lantern procession led by Anna Sueangam-iam, Miss Universe Thailand 2022; the Tak Loi Krathong Sai Festival, from November 21 to 24 along the Ping River, features a signature competition of 1,000 illuminated krathongs floating in continuous streams; Samut Songkhram's festival, from November 21 to 24, will illuminate the Mae Klong River with over 100,000 krathongs made from banana stalks; Sukhothai's festival runs from November 15 to 24; Chiang Mai's Yi Peng Festival runs from November 23 to 25, with authorised sky lantern releases on November 24 and 25; Roi Et's festival runs November 23 and 24 with a mass traditional dance of 11,101 participants on November 23; and the Authority expects approximately 6 billion baht in domestic tourism revenue during the Loi Krathong period, an 8 percent year-on-year increase, on an estimated 1.83 million domestic visitor trips, up 6 percent.

 SubjectiveThailand.go.th — the nationwide Loi Krathong 2026 calendarBangkok: the Tourism Authority of Thailand presents a nationwide calendar of Loi Krathong 2026 celebrations, featuring riverside ceremonies, illuminated historical landmarks and regional traditions; observed on the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month, the festival centres on floating decorated krathongs as an expression of gratitude and respect for water, and this year the full moon falls on November 24, with celebrations on different dates across the country; in Bangkok, the Rattanakosin Waterways festival runs from November 17 to 29, with Rama VIII Bridge from November 16 to 25, Phra Sumen Fort and Maha Kan Fort from November 23 to 25, and a historical route linking Wat Saket, Wat Ratchanatdaram, Wat Thepthidaram and Maha Kan Fort from November 17 to 29; Sukhothai's candlelight and fireworks festival runs from November 15 to 24 at Sukhothai Historical Park; Tak's Loi Krathong Sai, 1,000 floating krathongs, runs from November 21 to 24 at the foot of the Rattanakosin 200th Anniversary Bridge in Mueang Tak District; Chiang Saen's Yi Peng, Light of Faith on the Mekong, runs from November 20 to 24; Kamphaeng Phet's festival runs from November 16 to 24; Phuket's Loi Krathong by the Sea at Saphan Hin runs from November 16 to 25; Phang-nga's festival runs from November 19 to 28; and the calendar lists the Mae Klong banana-stem festival at Wat Phumarin Kudi Thong in Amphawa, Samut Songkhram, on November 24.

### Kyiv's Bridges Stand Closed in the BBC's Account and Partly Open in Kyiv's Own as Mr. Rutte Comes to Warsaw, California Subpoenas Nvidia in the Market's Quiet Hours, and the Strait Counts Eleven Crossings for Friday

Filed as: Edition No. 71 — The Overnight Watch · 2026-11-21T04:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-21-overnight-watch.html

The Night File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Kyiv’s Bridges Stand Closed in the BBC’s Account and Partly Open in Kyiv’s Own as Mr. Rutte Comes to Warsaw, California Subpoenas Nvidia in the Market’s Quiet Hours, and the Strait Counts Eleven Crossings for Friday

 The night file: a capital’s crossings closed in one account and carrying restricted traffic in another, with the Secretary General due in Warsaw today; a subpoena from California and an accounting inquiry over the chipmaker in the market’s quiet hours; eleven crossings counted in the strait for Friday against eight at Friday’s evening stamp, and a tanker still without a name; a grounded bulker on the Landes coast with 19 of its crew airlifted off; the text of Paris’s police law, still unpromulgated; and 300 buses rolling toward a bullring in Valencia. Saturday carries the Culture Feature.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Saturday, November 21, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 70, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 69, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Friday, from Edition No. 68, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Friday, and from Edition No. 67, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Friday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the overnight figures differ from the earlier figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Night in Brief: A Bridge Count That Will Not Agree With Itself, a Subpoena in the Quiet Hours, and Eleven Crossings

The night’s file is a capital whose bridges are closed in one account and carrying traffic in another, an alliance Secretary General on his way to Warsaw, a second legal front opened against the chipmaker while the market slept, and a strait count for Friday that rose after the evening stamp had fixed it at eight. The BBC’s updated file, carried in the BBC account filed below, reports Kyiv’s three struck bridges closed to traffic, against restricted traffic resumed in the assessment filed below and a crossing restored at 3 p.m. in the latest account filed below—the desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat and resolves none of it. Secretary General Rutte is due in Warsaw today, in the assessment and in the Council account filed below. California’s attorney general served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia on Thursday, in the crash account filed below, a fact that reached the overnight file after Friday’s close had already priced the accounting inquiry. The strait’s counter now puts Friday at eleven crossings, in the strait count filed below, against eight as of the evening stamp. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the night settled is the week’s close, which no overnight account reopens; the subpoena, which is a document and not a report; the strait’s revised Friday count; and the grounded bulker’s position on the Landes coast. What it left open is the rest: the bridges’ true state this morning, the alliance’s answer beyond a visit, Beijing’s word on the guardrails, the tanker’s name, the police law’s referral, and the router’s verdict, now eight days outstanding.

Kyiv and Warsaw at 0400: Nine Dead Confirmed in the Updated File, Three Bridges in Two States, and a Visitor Due Today

The updated British file fixes the night’s toll where the evening file left it rising. At least nine people were killed nationwide, seven in Kyiv and two in Lviv, with at least 28 injured, in the BBC account above, and Mayor Klitschko puts the capital’s toll at at least seven dead and 17 injured, in the same account; the Interior Minister’s figure of 30 injured across Ukraine stands beside it, in the latest account. The two killed outside the capital died in strikes on the Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, in the BBC account, and in Kharkiv a drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people and blowing out more than 50 windows, in the same account’s reporting of the mayor there. The package stands as the file has carried it: 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones, in the assessment, with strikes recorded at 23 locations, in the latest account, and the Western Ukrainian 750-kilovolt substation struck and the nuclear plants forced to reduce generation, in the same account.

On the bridges the night’s accounts divide, and the division is the fact. All three struck crossings—the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, the Darnytskyi and the Southern—have been closed to traffic, in the BBC account. Restricted traffic has resumed across the damaged bridges, in the assessment, and traffic across the Podilskyi crossing was restored at about 3 p.m. local time on Friday, in the latest account, with the Darnytskyi assessment continuing and the Pivdennyi partly restricted, in the same account. A third wire reading has the Podilskyi closed from the right bank to the left, the Darnytskyi damaged, and the Southern open only toward the right bank under the weight limits the file has carried all day, in the wire account filed below. The desk prints the three states in the Cocked Hat. No account in the overnight file describes the Darnytskyi’s structural damage, and none gives a repair timetable for any of the three.

In Poland the night added the alliance’s itinerary to the week’s words. Investigations stand open at the three fall sites—Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Molodycz—in the Council account, and Poland has formally requested additional allied assets, airborne early warning aircraft and F-35s among them, under Operation Eastern Sentry, in the Warsaw account filed below. That account’s headline has Poland invoking the alliance’s Article 4; its text describes urgent consultations with allies and the asset request, and no alliance statement in the file uses the article’s name—the desk prints the gap in the Cocked Hat. On the non-interception, the commander’s reason stands as the midnight file printed it: the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement, in the assessment. A second account puts the pilots’ window at about three minutes to identify and assess the objects before they came down in farmland, in the Warsaw account, and a third records that the command’s first warning signals came at 01:40 and that two early warning aircraft patrolled in the morning without an interception, in the drills account filed below. France’s foreign minister’s call for a meeting of the Security Council stands as Friday made it, in the Council account, and Poland’s foreign minister has signalled that Warsaw intends to raise the incident before the Council as well, in the Warsaw account. Mr. Rutte, who called the violations grave and clearly dangerous, is due in Warsaw today, in the barrage account filed below. Settled: the toll, the sites, the request, and the visit. Open: the bridges’ state, the Council’s meeting, and what the visit brings beyond solidarity.

New York at 0400: The Week Sleeps Where It Closed, and the Chipmaker’s File Gains a Subpoena

The market’s overnight is a quiet one, and the desk records the quiet as a quiet. No account in the file reopens Friday’s close: the Dow down 8.0 percent on the week, the S&P 500 down 8.6 percent, the Nasdaq Composite down 10.0 percent, and the chip index down 17.1 percent, its worst week since 2001, as the midnight file printed them. The week’s weight gained one figure overnight: the Nasdaq’s members lost more than $4 trillion in market value this week, in the wipeout account filed below, which records that by Friday afternoon most of the debut’s initial gain had washed away along with the index’s gains for the year. Friday night’s only forward readings are small and upward: the funds tracking the Dow, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 climbed 0.9, 1.0 and 1.5 percent in Friday-night trading, in the futures account filed below, and the futures themselves reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern, in the same account. One position was closed in the fall: the investor Michael Burry locked in profits on half of his bearish bets against Nvidia and against a fund tracking the semiconductor sector on Friday, in the wrap account filed below, which also puts Strategy, the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, down 30.3 percent on the week, the worst performance on the Nasdaq 100. The Friday detail stands in the wrap’s companion account filed below: AMD down another 13 percent after Thursday’s 8 percent on a short-seller report, CoreWeave down 12 percent, Nebius down 16 percent, and Micron, SanDisk and Western Digital down between 12 and 16 percent.

The chipmaker’s file, which Friday closed on a reported inquiry, gained a second legal front in the overnight reading—one dated Thursday, before the inquiry’s focus was reported. California’s attorney general, Mr. Bonta, served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia on Thursday in connection with Mr. Huang’s reported relationship, in the crash account above: “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information—and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Mr. Bonta said, in the same account. The federal inquiry stands where Reuters left it: enforcement staff scrutinising potential accounting issues, on the word of two people briefed on the matter, in the inquiry account filed below, with the Commission declining to comment and the company not immediately responding, in the same account. The reporting around both fronts centres on the same ground: the change last year in geographic revenue reporting, from billing addresses to customer headquarters, which removed Singapore from the breakdown as sales booked there rose toward half of global revenue, in the inquiry account, with $19.7 billion recorded in fiscal 2026 from customers headquartered in China, in the overnight account filed below, published at 1:10 a.m. Eastern today. The company’s only words in the file remain its interim chief’s from Tuesday’s earnings call—proud of the company’s role in supporting the industry, and more selective henceforward about industry financing deals, in the focus account filed below. No charges stand in the file on either front, and both accounts print the standing caution: an investigation is not evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action. Settled: the subpoena’s service and its stated scope, and the week’s close. Open: the company’s answer to either front, the inquiry’s scope, and the succession, on which the board’s position—no reinstatement intended, a search under way—stands unaltered.

Washington and Beijing at 0400: One Term, No Text, and No Word From Beijing in the File

The guardrails’ file did not move overnight, and the desk records what the file does and does not hold. The one concrete term stands as Secretary Bessent stated it on Friday: humans always involved in military decisions the technology touches, and no major military operation launched without a human being involved, in the Secretary’s account filed below, in the same words in the wire account filed below. No text, no timetable and no negotiating agency stands in the file, and no confirmation in Beijing’s own words stands in the overnight file either; the nearest parallel remains the embassy statement the week’s file carried, that the two sides should strengthen communication and keep the technology under human control. The chip half of the Secretary’s interview gained its machinery overnight: the Commerce Department’s steps on Monday extend the export restrictions to remote access, so that Chinese entities cannot rent computing power on overseas data centres to run advanced workloads, in the curbs account filed below. The H200 remains the most advanced chip China may purchase under licence, Chinese orders for it have been few, and Mr. Bessent put the Chinese stack “probably many years behind,” in the Secretary’s account; he also downplayed the differences between the Treasury and Commerce views, saying the administration’s officials are all committed to following the President’s instructions, in the same account. On the Huang question the two tellings stand unreconciled, as the midnight file printed them: discussed with President Xi, in the President’s telling; not raised in the bilateral, in the Secretary’s. Settled: the term as stated, and the curbs as described. Open: the text, Beijing’s confirmation, and how the human-involvement safeguard is to be applied in practice, which the curbs account names as its own watch line.

The Gulf at 0400: Eleven Crossings for Friday in the Revised Count, Four So Far on Saturday, and a Ship Still Without a Name

The strait’s counter revised Friday upward after the evening stamp had closed the day. Eleven commercial ships crossed on Friday, eight inbound and three outbound, three of them tankers, in the strait count above, against the eight the evening file carried as of 1802 UTC; four have crossed so far on Saturday, three inbound and one outbound, none of them tankers, as of 0759 UTC, with the container ship Tarlan the most recent, outbound at 0501 UTC, in the same count. The seven-day figure stands at 52 crossings, an average of 7.4 a day, about 9 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8, and the status stands severely restricted with the threat level severe, in the same count, which counts ships visible on the identification system and states plainly that ships sailing dark are missed. The week’s other instrument stands unreconciled beside it, as the midnight file printed it: 263 transits in the Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview, against the counter’s 47 for the same span it then covered. The desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat.

The tanker struck off Khasab on Friday afternoon ends the night as it ended the day: unnamed in every account in the file. The warning stands as Warning 214-26, a projectile on the port bow at about 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, a fire reported by the company security officer, no casualties and no environmental impact, in the tanker account filed below and in the wire account filed below. The Guards’ account gained a sentence overnight: the vessel was operating with support from the United States military, its navy said, blaming the incident on the ship’s use of an unauthorized passage and saying images of the explosion would be released later, in the Guards’ account filed below. No images stand in the file at the stamp, and the mine explanation remains unverified in every account that carries it. A separate encounter stands in the night’s maritime file: at 1102 UTC on Friday a skiff carrying six armed persons approached an eastbound bulk carrier in the recommended transit corridor, about 95 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla, under Warning 213-26, in the situation account filed below. Oil’s week stands as the midnight file closed it—Brent settled Friday at $92.57, the December contract at $83.98, both down on the week for a third straight week—and the OPEC+ ministers meet on November 29. Settled: the revised count and the week’s settlement. Open: the tanker’s name, flag, cargo and state; the weapon; the missing men of the week’s earlier ships; and the true count of the strait.

The night’s second ship is on the other side of the world and has a name. The bulk carrier Miro G, Malta-flagged, 169 metres and about 28,200 tonnes deadweight, built in 2011, lies aground on sand near Lit-et-Mixe on France’s Landes coast, where she came ashore at 00:55 local time on Friday after dragging both anchors in gusts of 48 knots from an emergency anchorage 1.8 nautical miles offshore, in the situation account and in the grounding account filed below. She was sailing in ballast from Bayonne toward Rouen, where tracking data put her to load 30,000 tonnes of wheat for Libya, in the capsize account filed below. Nineteen of her 22 crew were airlifted off by an Air and Space Force helicopter from Cazaux and taken to shelter at Saint-Julien-en-Born; three remain aboard to secure the ship, in the grounding account and in the rescue account filed below. The hull rests on the seabed, in the capsize account; the aim is a plan to refloat her by pulling her back out to sea and to prevent her capsizing as the tide changes, in the same account; she carries a little over a hundred tonnes of diesel, no pollution has been detected, the maritime response stands at its third level, the beach at Cap de l’Homy is closed, and a formal notice has gone to the shipowner, in the same accounts. No refloating stands in the file at the stamp. Settled: the position, the crew, and the plan. Open: the refloating, and the hull’s state when the tide turns.

Paris and Madrid at 0400: A Law’s Text, Still Unpromulgated, and a Bullring Filling at Noon

France’s file gained its text overnight and no new act. The law the Senate adopted on Friday by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting, creates a rebuttable presumption that national police officers and gendarmes used their firearms lawfully, in the text account filed below; it creates no new Penal Code defence and amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code, in the same account. Firearms use remains permitted in the five situations the article names, every use must remain absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate, the presumption does not cover municipal police, and any contrary evidence may rebut it at any time, in the same account. The Interior Minister’s position stands in both tellings: protection for officers in dangerous conditions, in the Paris account filed below, and, in the text account, that the measure does not authorise unrestricted shooting and prosecutors can still open investigations. Against it stand the United Nations rapporteur’s letter, as the file has carried it, and an opinion of November 5 from the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s democracy office recommending that the measure be reconsidered, in the text account. The law has not been promulgated and has not entered into force, in the same account; the Socialist group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation, and promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized, in the same account. No filing of the referral stands in the overnight file: the referral is promised, not yet made, as the midnight file left it. Settled: the vote and the text. Open: the referral, and the Council’s word.

Spain’s Saturday is a rally, and the night’s file carries its arrangements rather than its result. The People’s Party will mobilise about 300 buses to fill the Valencia bullring today, in the rally account filed below; the party’s Valencian organisation expects between 12,000 and 14,000 people, doors open at 10:30, the rally begins at noon, and Mr. Feij&oacute;o closes it, with the mayor of Valencia, Ms. Catal&aacute;, and the president of the Generalitat, Mr. P&eacute;rez Llorca, among the speakers, in the same account, whose speakers recall the party filling the same bullring in 1995 and in 2011. Mr. Feij&oacute;o’s Friday went to El Hierro in the Canary Islands, the campaign having replaced the Las Palmas rally with a visit to the island facing the arrival of thousands of people in small boats, in the campaign account filed below; Sunday takes him to Murcia and Monday to C&aacute;diz, in the same account. The debate’s verdict stands where Friday’s two polls put it—Mr. Feij&oacute;o the perceived winner, 51 to 29 and 43 to 33, before 10.2 million viewers, in the Madrid account filed below—and no post-debate voting-intention poll stands in the file. Spain votes on November 29, with the second debate agreed for about November 26. Settled: the arrangements and the verdict. Open: the bullring’s count, and whether any of it moves the vote.

The Air at 0400: No Root Cause in the Night’s File, and the Holiday Week at the Door

The promised announcement did not arrive in the night’s file either, and the desk records the standing at eight days. The agency’s question-and-answer briefing, updated on November 20, names the equipment for the first time in the file: it believes it addressed the initial cause by disabling the functionality of “the originating Juniper routers,” has disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers as a precaution, and has paused installing them, in the costs account filed below. The maker’s answer stands beside it in the same account: Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper Networks, said the equipment had operated according to its installed configuration. The briefing still says the agency and the contractor L3Harris are investigating the root cause, in the same account, and the overnight summaries hold the same line—preliminary findings pointing to overloaded legacy switches and router hardware generating the traffic, conclusions stressed as preliminary while the technical analysis completes, and no evidence of a malicious intrusion, in the holiday account filed below. The day’s count stands in the costs account at approximately 12,462 cancellations, of which the major airlines accounted for 9,082 and not all directly caused by the stop; the wider counts the week has carried stand in the Cocked Hat. The money stands estimated, not disclosed: about $345 million before tax for the four largest airlines, in one analyst’s estimate, against more than $1 billion for the industry in another’s, both carried in the costs account, and no airline has disclosed a figure, in the same account. Ahead of the file stands the holiday: the Port Authority projects 3.1 million passengers across its four New York and New Jersey airports between November 23 and 30, in the stop account filed below, and the Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers on November 23, the first day of that window. Settled: the equipment, the precaution, and the two sites. Open: the root cause itself, and whether the system that failed on November 13 carries the year’s heaviest week without a second failure.

Saturday Ahead: A Culture Feature, a Secretary General in Warsaw, and a Bullring at Noon

Saturday carries the paper’s Culture Feature, in the FT Weekend manner, filed ahead of the day’s watches. It also carries Mr. Rutte in Warsaw, the Valencia rally at noon, and the French left’s promised referral, whenever it is filed. The futures reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern. The week ahead carries the Senate Commerce Committee’s technical answers on the ground stop, due November 23; Alaska’s certification on November 25; Spain’s second debate, about November 26, and its vote on November 29; the OPEC+ ministers on November 29; the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 8 and 9; the end of government funding after December 11; and the Bank of Japan’s decision on December 18. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Kyiv’s bridges: all three closed to traffic, in the BBC’s updated file; restricted traffic resumed across the damaged bridges, in the assessment; the Podilskyi restored at about 3 p.m. and the Pivdennyi partly restricted, in the latest account; and the Podilskyi closed right bank to left bank with the Southern open only toward the right bank under weight limits, in the wire account. On Kyiv’s injured: 28 in the BBC’s file, 30 across Ukraine in the Interior Minister’s count, and 17 in Kyiv in the mayor’s. On the non-interception in Poland: the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement, in the operational commander’s account; a window of about three minutes to identify and assess, in the Warsaw account; and first warning signals at 01:40 with patrols flown and no interception, in the drills account. On the alliance’s procedure: Article 4 invoked, in the Warsaw account’s headline; urgent consultations and a formal request for additional assets, in its text; and no alliance statement in the file using the article’s name. On Anthropic’s Friday: down 8.5 percent to $88.91 in the wrap’s companion account and the Journal’s weekly account, against down 9.1 percent to $88.30 in the close account the midnight file carried. On the strait’s Friday: eleven crossings in the counter’s revised count, against eight as of 1802 UTC in the evening file’s reading of the same counter; and on its week, 52 crossings in the counter against 263 in the Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview. On the ground stop’s cancellations: approximately 12,462 on the day in the agency’s count, against about 18,000 cancelled after the stop in the week account the midnight file carried and more than 18,500 within, into or out of the United States by the morning of November 16 in the costs account’s reading. On its cost: about $345 million before tax for the four largest airlines in one estimate, against more than $1 billion for the industry in another. Inside the triangle is where the night honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

 SubjectiveBars Across — France Approves Rebuttable Presumption for Police Firearms UseFrance has approved a bill creating a rebuttable presumption that National Police officers and gendarmes used firearms lawfully. The Senate adopted it on November 20 by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting; the National Assembly approved the text in July. It has not yet been promulgated or entered into force. The measure creates no new Penal Code defence; it amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code. Firearms use remains permitted in five situations, and every use must remain absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate. The presumption covers national police and gendarmes, not municipal police, and any contrary evidence may rebut it at any time. The Interior Minister said the measure does not authorise unrestricted shooting and prosecutors can still open investigations. An opinion issued on November 5 by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights recommended reconsidering the measure. The Socialist group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation; promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized.

 SubjectiveNomad Lawyer — FAA Ground Stop: 12,462 Flights Cancelled Before ThanksgivingThe nationwide ground stop of November 13 resulted in 12,462 flight cancellations. The disruption began at about 3:30 p.m. Eastern on November 13, manifesting as instability in the telecommunications infrastructure; instability was reported across 17 of the 22 en route centres. The network was overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The agency identified two primary points of origin: a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas. The ground stop was lifted by 8:15 p.m. that evening, and about 3,500 airborne aircraft landed safely. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey projects a throughput of 3.1 million passengers across its four major airports between November 23 and 30.

 SubjectiveTravel Market News — FAA Ground Stop Cause: Router Probe and Airline CostsThe investigation into the November 13 ground stop centres on a newly installed router at a remote radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. In its November 20 update the agency’s question-and-answer briefing names the equipment: it believes it addressed the initial cause by disabling the functionality of “the originating Juniper routers,” has disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system as a precaution, and has paused installing them. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper Networks, said the equipment had operated according to its installed configuration. The briefing still says the agency and the contractor are investigating the root cause. The agency’s count puts cancellations on the day at approximately 12,462 flights, of which major airlines accounted for 9,082, and not all were directly caused by the stop. Bernstein puts the cost to the four largest airlines at about $345 million before tax; Bloomberg says airlines could lose more than $1 billion.

 SubjectiveThe Traveler — How the Nov. 13 FAA Ground Stop Shapes 2026 Holiday TravelA rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 has intensified scrutiny of the air traffic control network just as tens of millions of travellers head into the Thanksgiving and Christmas rush, with operations largely back to normal but political fallout and lingering disruption risks shaping how airlines and passengers plan the holidays. Federal statements attribute the disruption to problems within ageing network infrastructure interacting with ongoing modernisation work, not to a cyberattack. Early findings point to overloaded legacy switches and router hardware at several sites generating unusually high volumes of network traffic. Officials stress that these conclusions remain preliminary while contractors and federal investigators complete a technical root-cause analysis. Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford have both emphasised that there is currently no evidence of a malicious intrusion.
